title: Universe in Pi
content_html:
Universe in Pi

Is the whole universe, past and future, encoded into pi?

In a very weak, formal sense — but almost certainly not in any useful or meaningful way.

A common (popular) claim is: because π has infinitely many non-repeating digits, it must contain every possible finite string of digits (so, somewhere in its decimal expansion you’ll find your name encoded in ASCII, the text of Hamlet, etc.). If π were normal (a technical property meaning every finite digit-block appears with the expected frequency), that would imply every finite string appears somewhere in π. But we do not know whether π is normal — it’s strongly believed, and statistical tests of trillions of digits are consistent with normality, but there’s no proof.

Even if π contains every finite string, that only means somewhere in the digits you can find a finite block equal to any finite message you like if you choose a mapping from digits to letters. That does not make the digits semantically meaningful, and it doesn’t give you any way to know where the block is except by searching. Practically speaking the positions involved could be astronomically large (far beyond any feasible search). Popular pieces that repeat the “π contains everything” idea are describing this statistical/poetic possibility, not a usable encoding.

Saying “π contains the whole universe, past and future” is much stronger than “π contains every finite string.” To represent an entire history of the universe as an exact, lossless object would require either (a) a finite description (a finite string) that fully determines that history, or (b) an infinite object encoding infinitely many bits. If the whole history can be written as a finite string, then — under normality/disjunctivity assumptions — that finite string might appear somewhere in π. But we have no reason to believe the full, exact physical history compresses into any reasonably short finite string. If the universe’s complete history requires genuinely infinite, uncomputable information (for example, solutions to undecidable problems or uncomputable reals), then a computable constant like π cannot encode those uncomputable bits in any algorithmically retrievable way. π is computable (there are algorithms to produce its digits), so it is not Martin-Löf (algorithmically) random and cannot serve as an oracle for uncomputable truths.

Mathematicians have constructed numbers (e.g., Chaitin’s Ω — the halting-probability constant) whose bits encode answers to the halting problem; such numbers are algorithmically random and contain enormous uncomputable information. But they are uncomputable — you cannot actually list their digits by an algorithm — so they’re not a practically accessible “book of the universe” either. π is computable and not the sort of incompressible, uncomputable number (like Chaitin’s Ω) that would encode arbitrary uncomputable facts in an accessible way.

If pi is infinite, it therefore contains itself?

People sometimes imagine π as a never-ending library of digits. If so, shouldn’t it somewhere include the string of digits that is itself? In other words, could the infinite decimal expansion of π appear as a substring within π?

Finite vs. infinite strings

  • Finite strings: Any finite sequence of digits (like “314159”) could in principle occur somewhere in π (if π is normal or at least disjunctive — both unproven but widely believed).
  • Infinite strings: An infinite sequence cannot appear as a substring inside another infinite sequence unless the two are identical from some position onward.

So the infinite decimal expansion of π cannot “occur inside itself” as a proper substring, because that would mean π repeats itself at some point — which would make it periodic, and π is provably not periodic. Every finite prefix of π (say the first million digits) trivially appears in π — right at the start! And if π is normal, then copies of those finite prefixes should also appear elsewhere, scattered throughout the expansion. So in that limited sense, π “contains” its own finite pieces again and again.

Self-reference vs. self-containment

This is like the difference between:

A sentence quoting a few of its own words (possible, like “This sentence has six words”),
versus
A sentence containing its entire infinite self (impossible, because you’d never finish writing it).

π cannot contain its own entire infinite expansion as a substring, because that would require repetition and periodicity. But π does, of course, contain all of its finite prefixes, and if it’s normal, those prefixes should recur infinitely often within it.

Infinity

In mathematics, infinity is not a number but a concept. It’s used in several ways:

  • Potential infinity: an endless process (e.g., keep adding 1 forever).
  • Actual infinity: treating an infinite set (like all natural numbers) as a complete object.

Set theory (Cantor, 19th c.) showed there are different sizes of infinity (countable, uncountable). Mathematicians routinely use infinity in analysis (limits, calculus) and set theory without contradiction — it’s internally consistent within established axiomatic systems (like Zermelo–Fraenkel with Choice, ZFC). So in pure math, infinity is a formal tool, not a flaw.

Physics is about describing the empirical world. Here, infinities often signal problems:

  • Infinities in equations (like quantum field theory divergences) are usually “renormalized away.”
  • Cosmology debates whether the universe is finite or infinite in extent — but we cannot observe an actual infinity; we only ever measure finite quantities.

Mathematics ≠ physics: Maths builds abstract structures; physics decides which of them describe reality. We use imaginary numbers, n-dimensional spaces, and even perfect circles — none exist physically, but they’re indispensable tools. The real world may never realize an infinite quantity, but treating processes as if they extend to infinity (limits, continuity) gives extremely accurate predictions. So rather than a flaw, infinity might be a necessary abstraction: a way to model processes and structures that have no neat finite expression. The “flaw” appears only if you mistake the abstraction for physical reality. In physics, infinities are red flags: they tell us our theories are being pushed beyond their valid range.

Why infinity is essential to calculus

When we define a derivative (the slope of a curve), we say:

f′(x) = lim(h → 0) [ f(x + h) − f(x) ] / h

This is not saying we actually set h = 0 (which would cause division by zero). Instead, we imagine shrinking h smaller and smaller — forever. Infinity (or more precisely, an infinite process) is what makes the definition rigorous.

The area under a curve is defined as:

∫ from a to b f(x) dx = lim(n → ∞) Σ(i = 1 to n) f(x_i) · Δx

We approximate the area with rectangles. As we take infinitely many rectangles (n \to \infty), the error shrinks to zero. Again, infinity is not “real rectangles” in the world, but a way to guarantee exactness. Without infinity, you’d always be stuck with approximations (finite steps, finite sums). Infinity allows math to guarantee that derivatives and integrals converge to exact values. That’s why calculus lets us compute planetary orbits, design circuits, and predict quantum behavior with astonishing accuracy — even though the real world never “uses” infinity directly. Infinity is mathematical scaffolding: it lets us describe continuous change with finite rules.

If mind and memory are essentially probabilistic, how is it possible for them to create and maintain a formal and consistent system such as mathematics?

The mind and memory are indeed probabilistic, but precisely because of redundancy, abstraction, and cultural error-correction, they can bootstrap formal and consistent systems. Mathematics is not proof that our brains are deterministic — it is proof that probabilistic systems, properly scaffolded, can converge on reliability.

Neurons and synapses fire with probabilistic variability (release probability < 1 at many synapses; noise in spike timing). Memory recall is also reconstructive and prone to error. But when many noisy elements combine, statistical laws allow stable patterns to emerge — just as a noisy crowd can clap in rhythm, or millions of transistors with occasional errors still form a functioning computer. This is redundancy and error correction at work. Our brains can approximate rules from patterns, even if individual instances are noisy. This is a hallmark of learning systems. Mathematics exploits this: once we abstract “2 apples + 2 apples = 4 apples,” we can detach the concept of 2 from the apples.

The probabilistic substrate thus gives rise to generalization capacity, which underlies abstraction. Whilst a noisy substrate might seem incapable of producing something as exact as mathematics, the very same probabilistic dynamics allow for flexibility, adaptation, and redundancy. The system is unreliable in detail but robust in the whole. From this substrate, patterns emerge. Brains have evolved to extract regularities from noisy input, in effect, the brain turns probabilistic experiences into repeatable concepts. The fuzziness of experience gives rise to the clarity of rules.

Humans have also invented external supports — writing, diagrams, symbols — that let us offload memory and check reasoning, effectively a social error-correction system. No single brain has to be perfect; the community checks and re-checks arguments until consensus is reached. By standardizing how we write numbers, equations, and logic, we constrain the variability of thought. This reduces the impact of probabilistic “noise” from memory and perception, stabilising mathematics across centuries, but which is continuously reconstructed and stabilized by fallible, probabilistic minds.
